extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, intellectual property professionals, and biotechnology industry stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and historical legal standards for obtaining and assessing patent protection for biotechnology inventions (microorganisms, transgenic animals, genetic processes) under U.S. law, with attention to PTO practice and appellate precedent. Useful for counsel deciding claim strategy and jurisdictional filing decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court in Diamond v. Chakrabarty held that a live, man-made microorganism is patentable subject matter under Section 101; the principle articulated was that “anything under the sun that is made by man” is eligible for patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Chakrabarty as controlling U.S. precedent for patenting genetically engineered microorganisms and similar biotechnological inventions. The article recounts the Court’s focus on whether the claimed microorganism constituted a “manufacture” or “composition of matter.” Quote and rely on the broad congressional mandate regarding patentable subject matter embodied in §101 when evaluating biotech inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-naturally occurring non-human multicellular organisms are patentable (PTO position)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO stated (April 7, 1988) that it “now considers non-naturally occurring non-human multicellular living organisms, including animals, to be patentable subject matter within the scope of 35 U.S.C. 101.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on the PTO’s policy and subsequent allowance history (e.g., Harvard Mouse) when prosecuting claims to transgenic animals and other non-natural higher life forms in the U.S. Cite Ex Parte Allen and PTO notices to show consistency with agency precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of human intervention / non-natural occurrence as a factual basis for eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: In Ex Parte Allen the Board reversed an examiner’s rejection of genetically engineered oysters because it found “no evidence that the claimed polyploid oysters occur naturally without the intervention of man.” The presence (or absence) of evidence that the subject matter occurs in nature is pivotal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking protection for organisms or multicellular life forms, emphasize factual showing that the claimed organism does not occur in nature (human manipulation, transgenic features, non‑natural ploidy, engineered plasmid combinations). Use experimental data, breeding records, and molecular characterization to establish non-natural origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple claim types (method, composition, organism) as prosecution strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Chakrabarty’s application contained three groups of claims: (1) the method of producing the bacterium, (2) an inoculum composed of a carrier material and the bacterium, and (3) the genetically engineered bacterium itself; the PTO allowed the first two but initially rejected the organism claim under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft and pursue diverse claim types (process/method claims, compositions/mixtures, and organism/product claims) because different claim categories may fare differently under eligibility and examination. If a product claim faces a §101 objection, rely on method or composition claims as alternative protection and prosecute all groups in parallel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability is judged on novelty and nonobviousness, not morality
rubrics_metrics.description: The article states: “The role of the Patent Office is to determine novelty and nonobviousness; issues of morality and ethics are best left to other organizations” and that patents themselves are not designed to address moral/ethical objections to manufacturing living things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing filings and responding to office actions, focus arguments and evidence on statutory criteria such as novelty (35 U.S.C. §102) and nonobviousness (35 U.S.C. §103). Expect that moral or ethical objections are not proper grounds for denying statutory patentability in the PTO; address policy concerns separately with stakeholders if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional variance in eligibility (national differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all countries follow the U.S. approach to patenting higher life forms; for example, Canada refused to patent the Harvard Mouse—the Supreme Court of Canada ruled it was not patentable subject matter under the Canadian Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess patent strategy globally: evaluate domestic eligibility rules and relevant case law in each jurisdiction before filing. Don’t assume U.S. precedent will be accepted abroad; tailor claims and arguments to national statutes and precedent (and consider parallel filings, defensive strategies, or trade‑secret options where foreign eligibility is doubtful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of patentable biotechnology subject matter (processes, organisms, engineered crops, cell-line methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article catalogs successful patents: PCR process patents (amplifying DNA), genetically engineered crops (herbicide-resistant seeds), transgenic animals (Harvard Mouse), and methods for isolating embryonic stem cells (Thomson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories as precedent that processes, compositions, genetically modified organisms, and methods for deriving and sustaining cell lines can be claimed and obtained in the U.S. Provide detailed enabling disclosure for these categories and anticipate prior art challenges specific to each technology (e.g., molecular process prior art for PCR; sequence/construct prior art for transgenics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of claim drafting skill in defining patent scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors note that “The patents for these innovations are limited only by the skill of the individuals drafting the claims,” implying that claim drafting determines the effective breadth and enforceability of biotech patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in precise, thoughtful claim drafting: define scope to cover commercially important embodiments while providing adequate support and enablement in the specification. Anticipate infringement/invalidity arguments and craft dependent claims and claim charts to tie claims to technical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural recourse: examiner rejections can be appealed and reversed
rubrics_metrics.description: Chakrabarty’s examiner rejected organism claims under §101; the Board affirmed, the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals reversed, and the Supreme Court ultimately granted certiorari and decided in favor of patentability. This shows an appellate pathway from examiner through Board and higher courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When faced with adverse examiner findings on eligibility, novelty, or other grounds, consider administrative appeals (BPAI/PTAB), appeals to the Federal Circuit/CCPA (historically), and, in rare cases, certiorari. Use strong legal and factual records at the PTO level to preserve issues for appeal.
